Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no “Is the lung healthy?” answer and the rationale cites a specific device or incidental finding—such as a “left-sided vascular catheter”—but no recorded tool observation explicitly documents that object in the same image.

Observable verification action: Check the raw tool observations for an explicit mention of the same object and attribute, and confirm it is relevant to the lung field. If no observation supports it, do not present it as observed evidence; base the yes/no answer and rationale only on documented lung/parenchymal findings, or consult/obtain the missing observation. Confirm the final polarity matches those documented findings. In this case, “No” matched the released reference, but the catheter rationale was not supported by any recorded observation, so the correct grade alone does not verify the evidence path. Options were empty, so no option-letter mapping check was needed.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no answer to “Is [organ] healthy?” and the draft rationale cites specific imaging findings—but the current trajectory does not show those findings in a raw tool observation.

Observable verification action: Re-read the available image/report/tool outputs and confirm that each cited finding is actually present and addresses the same organ and attribute asked about. For “Is the lung healthy?”, require at least one explicit lung-relevant abnormality, such as a lung nodule, before answering “No”; do not rely on an adjacent or unrelated finding such as prior sternotomy alone. If the named finding is not confirmed, revise the rationale or answer to match the observed evidence. Here options are empty, so no letter-text mapping is needed; if options were displayed, map the supported answer text to the listed choice and check that its letter and text agree.

Trigger: Finalizing a comparative organ-abnormality answer such as “Which organ is abnormal, heart or lung?” when the terminal rationale cites a grounded imaging report.

Observable verification action: Locate the raw grounded-report statement for each candidate organ. Choose the organ only if its statement contains an explicit abnormal finding (for example, “mildly prominent cardiac silhouette” or “cardiomegaly”) and the other organ’s statement is explicitly negative or normal (for example, “lungs are free of infiltrates and masses”). Do not infer a heart abnormality from a normal-lung statement alone. If the raw tool observation containing the cited report phrase is absent from the transcript, do not treat the correct final grade as proof of the evidence procedure; retrieve or rerun the grounded report/verify step first. If options are displayed, map the supported organ text back to the displayed choice and confirm the letter and text agree. In this case no options were present, so the relevant check is evidence attribution: the answer “heart” is supported only if the grounded report actually names the cardiac abnormality while clearing the lungs.
